links.note: 467 says to think and then resolve (எண்ணித் துணிக) and calls it a lapse to say 'we will think after resolving'. 671 takes up where that ends: deliberation's end is reaching resolve (சூழ்ச்சி முடிவு துணிவெய்தல்), and the fault now is letting that resolve sit in delay (தாழ்ச்சியுள் தங்குதல் தீது). Read together they bracket the moment of decision: no acting before it, no lingering after it.

668, in the chapter on firmness in action, says to carry out a deed seen with an unconfused mind without wavering and with delay driven off (தூக்கங் கடிந்து செயல்). 671 makes the same claim from the side of method: resolve that stays in delay (தாழ்ச்சி) is a fault. The pairing shows the book treating promptness after decision both as a trait of character and as a rule of procedure.

671 calls it a fault when a resolved deed lingers in delay (தாழ்ச்சியுள் தங்குதல் தீது). 672 immediately limits this: there are deeds to be done slowly, and over those one should take time (தூங்குக தூங்கிச் செயற்பால); only the deed that must be done without delay must not be slept on. Delay is therefore wrong by the nature of the task, not in itself.

383 lists தூங்காமை, not delaying, among three things that never leave a ruler. 672 uses the same verb to say தூங்குக for some tasks and தூங்கற்க for others. Parimelazhagar makes the connection himself, saying that what 383 stated as தூங்காமை is here divided into its cases.

490 says to be like the heron in the season for folding up (கூம்பும் பருவத்து) and like its strike when the moment is right (சீர்த்த இடத்து). 672 gives the same double instruction without the image: take time over what is to be done slowly, and do not delay what must not be delayed. Both hold that waiting and speed are each correct in their place.

33 tells one to do deeds of virtue by whatever means are possible (ஒல்லும் வகையான்) and wherever they can go (செல்லும்வாய் எல்லாம் செயல்). 673 uses the same pair of words for statecraft: wherever it is possible the deed is good (ஒல்லும்வாய் எல்லாம் வினைநன்றே), and where it is not, act by looking for the way that will go (செல்லும்வாய் நோக்கிச் செயல்). The same formula of the possible and the passable serves virtue in Book 1 and policy in Book 2. (The first word of 673 is misprinted in this edition; the commentaries read ஒல்லும்.)

485 says those who have the world in mind wait, unshaken, with their mind on the time (காலம் கருதி இருப்பர்). Manakkudavar reads the second half of 673 in that sense: when the deed is not possible, keep it in mind and act on seeing the place where it becomes possible. Parimelazhagar reads 673 differently, as open force where one is stronger and one of the other three expedients where one is not, so the link holds on Manakkudavar's reading.

879 says to cut a thorn tree while it is young, because grown hard it wounds the hand that cuts (கைகொல்லும் காழ்த்த இடத்து). 674 says what is left over (எச்சம்) of an enmity, like what is left of a fire, scorches later (தீயெச்சம் போலத் தெறும்). Both hold that an enemy not dealt with completely grows; one uses a tree and the other an ember.

612 warns against letting a task die in the doing, on the ground that the world leaves those who leave work unfinished (வினைக்குறை தீர்ந்தாரின் தீர்ந்தன்று உலகு). 674 gives a different ground for the same rule: the unfinished remainder of a task (வினை ... எச்சம்) is not inert but, like the remnant of a fire, comes back to destroy. 612 names the social cost of unfinished work and 674 the danger in the remainder itself.

631 defines the minister as one excellent in means, time, manner of doing and the hard deed itself (கருவியும் காலமும் செய்கையும் செய்யும் அருவினையும்). 675 lists resources, means, time, deed and place (பொருள் கருவி காலம் வினை இடனொடு ஐந்தும்) as what must be thought through before acting. The lists overlap in கருவி, காலம் and வினை, so 675 reads as the minister's competence of 631 turned into a procedure, with resources and place added.

471 says to weigh four strengths before acting: of the deed, oneself, the opponent and the allies (தூக்கிச் செயல்). 675 gives a second checklist of five ending in the same way (எண்ணிச் செயல்). Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar gloss each of the five in 675 as two-sided, one's own and the enemy's, which is the comparison 471 asks for, applied item by item.

461 says to act after considering what will be lost, what will come of it, and the gain it yields later (அழிவதூஉம் ஆவதூஉம் ... ஊதியமும் சூழ்ந்து செயல்). 676 says to act after looking at the completion, the hindrance, and the large yield once it is finished (முடிவும் இடையூறும் ... படுபயனும் பார்த்துச் செயல்). Both are a three-part weighing of cost against return placed before action; Parimelazhagar reads முடிவு in 676 as the effort needed to finish, which brings it close to 461's 'what is lost'.

462 says nothing is hard to attain for those who act after examining a matter with chosen company (தெரிந்த இனத்தொடு) and thinking it over themselves. 677 narrows whose counsel counts for a particular task: the one who knows that deed from inside (அவ்வினை உள்ளறிவான்), whom Parimelazhagar takes to be someone who has done it before. General consultation in 462 becomes, in 677, learning the mind of the person with experience of the task.

678 says to get one deed done by means of another, as one binds an elephant with a rutting elephant (யானையால் யானையாத் தற்று). Manakkudavar takes this as setting an enemy's own enemy against him. On that reading 875 is the case worked out: one who is alone with two enemies should take one of them as an ally (இன்துணையாக் கொள்க அவற்றின் ஒன்று). Parimelazhagar reads 678 more generally, as making a task in hand the means to another like it.

Both verses explain how a deed (வினை) is made easy through an elephant scene. In 758 one who acts with wealth in hand is like a man watching an elephant fight from a hilltop (குன்றேறி யானைப் போர் கண்டற்று), safe above the danger; in 678 one deed is used on another as a tame elephant is used to bind a wild one. The elephant stands in each for the dangerous size of the undertaking, handled once from a distance and once by using its own kind.

633 lists three abilities of a minister side by side: dividing, keeping one's own close, and joining those who had separated (பிரித்தலும் பேணிக் கொளலும் பிரிந்தார்ப் பொருத்தலும்). 679 ranks two such tasks: bringing the unallied over (ஒட்டாரை ஒட்டிக் கொளல்) is more urgent (விரைந்ததே) than doing good to friends. What 633 gives as a list of skills, 679 puts in order of urgency.

875 says that one without allies and facing two enemies should take one of them as a pleasing ally. 679 says that winning over ஒட்டார் is more urgent than favours to friends; Manakkudavar takes ஒட்டார் as one's enemies, Parimelazhagar as those not allied with one's enemy. On either reading both verses treat alliance as something to be made out of the hostile or uncommitted when one is pressed.

874 says the world rests in the greatness of the person of character who lives treating enmity as friendship (பகைநட்பாக் கொண்டொழுகும்). 679 states the same move as a priority in conducting a task: making the ஒட்டார் one's own comes before kindness to friends. 874 praises it as character (பண்பு) while 679 prescribes it as urgent policy.

861 says to avoid standing against the strong (வலியார்க்கு மாறேற்றல் ஓம்புக). 680 describes what that means for a weak party: those of small domain, fearing the trembling of their own side (உள்நடுங்கல் அஞ்சி), bow to the greater and accept terms if they can get them (குறைபெறின் கொள்வர் பெரியார்ப் பணிந்து). 861 gives the rule and 680 the settlement that follows from it.

488 says to bear with enemies on meeting them (செறுநரைக் காணின் சுமக்க), for when their end comes their head will go down; Parimelazhagar glosses சுமக்க as bowing. 680 has the small bow to the great to obtain terms. 488 adds what 680 does not say: that such bowing can be a way of waiting for the stronger side's fall.

967, on honour, says it is better to be called ruined as one stands than to live by going behind those who are hostile to one (ஒட்டார்பின் சென்று வாழ்தலின்). 680 says the small will bow to the great and take what terms they can. The conflict depends on reading 967's ஒட்டார் as covering a stronger enemy; Parimelazhagar limits it to following scorners for a living, but he also remarks on 680 that bowing is not the wish of those with honour, which is why the verse says 'they will accept' as a report of worldly practice.

The first line of 681 and of 992 is the same: அன்புடைமை ஆன்ற குடிப்பிறத்தல். 992 says these two are what is called courtesy (பண்புடைமை என்னும் வழக்கு); 681 lists them and adds a third, the qualities kings desire (வேந்தவாம் பண்புடைமை), as the nature of one who carries a message. The envoy's qualification is thus the book's general definition of courtesy with a courtly requirement added.

681 asks of the envoy 'qualities that kings desire' (வேந்தவாம் பண்புடைமை) without saying what they are. Manakkudavar glosses the phrase as not desiring what the king desires, which is the content of 692 (மன்னர் விழைப விழையாமை), and Parimelazhagar says this quality is obtained from the following chapter on conduct around kings. 692 therefore supplies, on the commentators' reading, what 681 leaves unstated.

502 places trust in one born in a good family (குடிப்பிறந்து), free of faults and with a shame that recoils from blemish. 681 makes birth in a fit family (ஆன்ற குடிப்பிறத்தல்) one of the envoy's three marks. Family is used in both as evidence about a person before he is given a charge, for trust in general in 502 and for the embassy in 681.

513 says trust belongs with one who has love, understanding, clarity and freedom from desire (அன்பறிவு தேற்றம் அவாவின்மை). 682 opens with the same two words and names the envoy's indispensable three as love, understanding and considered skill in speech (அன்பறிவு ஆராய்ந்த சொல்வன்மை). The envoy starts from the same base as any trusted officer, and what is particular to his office is speech; Parimelazhagar glosses அன்பு in both verses as love for the king.

722 says those who can make what they have learned go home before the learned are called learned among the learned (கற்றாருள் கற்றார்). 683 uses the same construction for the envoy: he must be strong in the treatises among those who know treatises (நூலாருள் நூல்வல்லன்). Both measure learning by standing among the learned, not against the unlearned.

683 sets two groups side by side: among spear-bearers (வேலாருள்) the envoy speaks of victory, and among treatise-knowers (நூலாருள்) he is master of the treatise. 727 pairs the same two things as a simile: the treatise learned by one who fears the assembly is a bright sword in the hand of a பேடி among enemies. In both the treatise is treated as the speaker's weapon, and 727 adds that it is useless without the nerve to use it.

636 asks what subtle scheme can stand before those who have keen intelligence together with the treatises (மதிநுட்பம் நூலோடு உடையார்க்கு). 684 requires of the envoy understanding and well-examined learning (அறிவு ... ஆராய்ந்த கல்வி) held together. Parimelazhagar glosses the first term in each verse as natural intelligence and the second as acquired learning, so both verses ask for the two in combination, for the minister and for the envoy.

684 counts presence (உரு) among the three things an envoy needs. 407 says the fine looks of one without fine, penetrating understanding are those of a well-made clay doll (மண்மாண் புனைபாவை). 407 supplies the limit on 684's உரு: appearance counts only in the union (செறிவு) with understanding and learning that 684 itself demands.

667 says not to scorn anyone on seeing their form (உருவுகண்டு எள்ளாமை வேண்டும்), since there are people like the linchpin of a great chariot. 684 makes form (உரு) a requirement for going on an embassy. The two can stand together if 667 is about judging capacity for work and 684 about the first impression at a foreign court, but 667 limits how far 684's criterion should be carried beyond that office.

649 says those who cannot say a few faultless words long to say many (பலசொல்லக் காமுறுவர் ... சிலசொல்லல் தேற்றாதவர்). 685 begins its description of the envoy with speaking in gathered, brief form (தொகச் சொல்லி). Brevity is treated in both as the mark of command of speech, and 685 makes it a working requirement of the envoy.

696 tells one who serves a king to say what is needed and not disliked, in a way that is wanted (வெறுப்பில வேண்டுப வேட்பச் சொலல்). 685 has the envoy remove what offends and speak so as to please (தூவாத நீக்கி நகச்சொல்லி) while securing good for his own side. The same manner of speech is prescribed toward one's own king in 696 and toward a foreign king in 685; in both the pleasing manner serves what has to be said.

585 describes the spy as one who does not fear the eye (கண்ணஞ்சாது) and never lets anything out. 686 describes the envoy as கண் அஞ்சான், one who does not fear the eye. Parimelazhagar glosses both as not flinching from an angry, searching look. The king's two agents abroad share this mark, though the spy must stay silent under the look and the envoy must go on speaking.

647 says one who is able in speech, makes no slip and has no fear (சொலல்வல்லன் சோர்விலன் அஞ்சான்) is hard for anyone to defeat. 686 gives the envoy the same combination: he speaks so that it goes home (செலச்சொல்லி) and does not fear (அஞ்சான்), with learning and a sense of timing added. 647 states the general claim about speech and 686 applies it to the embassy.

724 says to make what one has learned go home before the learned (கற்றார்முன் கற்ற செலச்சொல்லி). 686 uses the same two terms for the envoy: having learned (கற்று), he speaks so that it goes home (செலச்சொல்லி). In both, learning is complete only when it can be delivered to a demanding audience, the assembly in 724 and a hostile court in 686.

696 tells the courtier to read the king's mood and consider the time (குறிப்பறிந்து காலங் கருதி) before speaking. 687 has the best envoy know what is due, consider the time (காலங் கருதி) and know the place before he speaks. The phrase காலங் கருதி is common to both, so the discipline for speaking to one's own king is the same as for speaking to another's.

675 says to act after thinking through resources, means, time, deed and place (காலம் ... இடனொடு ... எண்ணிச் செயல்). 687 uses the same terms for speech: consider the time, know the place, think it through and then speak (காலங் கருதி இடனறிந்து எண்ணி உரைப்பான்). The envoy's speech is planned by the same checklist the book gives for any deed.

712 says those who know how words work should discern the opening (இடைதெரிந்து), understand well and then speak; Parimelazhagar takes இடை as the receptive moment of the assembly. 687 asks the envoy to consider the time, which Parimelazhagar likewise glosses as the listener's receptive state (செவ்வி). Both make the listener's readiness a condition of speaking.

501 says a man is to be trusted after being tested by virtue, wealth, pleasure and fear for life. 688 lists the faithful envoy's marks as purity, support, resolve and truthfulness (தூய்மை துணைமை துணிவுடைமை ... வாய்மை). Parimelazhagar explains தூய்மை as being clean in respect of wealth and pleasure and துணிவு as not holding back for fear of harm, which makes 688's qualities the passes of 501's tests.

298 says outer purity comes by water and inner purity is seen through truth (அகந்தூய்மை வாய்மையால் காணப்படும்). 688 names தூய்மை first among the envoy's marks and then requires வாய்மை along with all three. 298 gives the reason the two words belong together: truthfulness is how inner purity shows.

383 names three things that never leave a ruler: promptness, learning and resolve (தூங்காமை கல்வி துணிவுடைமை இம்மூன்றும்). 688 has the same frame for the envoy who repeats the king's message: purity, support and resolve, these three (தூய்மை துணைமை துணிவுடைமை இம்மூன்றின்). துணிவுடைமை is the term common to king and envoy; the other two differ with the office.

139 says that for people of good conduct it is not possible to speak evil with the mouth even by a slip (வழுக்கியும் வாயாற் சொலல்). 689 asks the same of the envoy in his own field: a firmness whose mouth does not let slip a word that brings blemish (வடுமாற்றம் வாய்சோரா). What Book 1 treats as a result of character, 689 makes a condition for carrying the king's word. (This edition prints வாய்சேரா; the commentaries read வாய்சோரா.)

642 says to guard against a lapse in speech (சொல்லின்கட் சோர்வு) because both gain and ruin come from it. 689 is that rule at the point where the stakes are the king's: the envoy must not let a word that discredits slip from his mouth (வாய்சோரா); Parimelazhagar adds that the slip in question would come from fear for himself. The verb சோர் is shared, and 689 names the hardness (வன்கண்) that prevents the lapse 642 warns of.

778 says warriors who do not fear for their life when battle comes (உறின் உயிர் அஞ்சா மறவர்) do not lose their distinction even if their lord is angry. 690 says the envoy is one who, even if it brings his end (இறுதி பயப்பினும்), does not fall short and secures what is good for his lord (இறைவற்கு உறுதி). The envoy's office is given the soldier's standard, with both verses naming the lord (இறைவன்) as the one served.

638 says that even if the king destroys good counsel and knows nothing himself, the one at his side owes it to him to say what is good for him (உறுதி ... கூறல் கடன்). 690 says the envoy secures the lord's good (உறுதி) even at the cost of his own life. Both use உறுதி for the king's real interest and hold the servant to it under threat, from his own king in 638 and from a foreign one in 690.

723 says those who will die among enemies are easy to find and those who do not fear in an assembly are rare (பகையகத்துச் சாவார் எளியர் அரியர் அவையகத்து அஞ்சாதவர்). 690 asks the envoy to face death (இறுதி) while speaking in a hostile court. 723 separates the two kinds of courage and rates the second as rarer; the envoy of 690 needs both together, which indicates how much the verse asks.
